newsitem.title: FRANCE: France shows will to qualify for EMU - economists.
newsitem.headline: France shows will to qualify for EMU - economists.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government has shown its determination to qualify for European monetary union with its emergency 1997 deficit-cutting package, boosting taxes on big business, economists said on Monday.
The decision to raise corporate taxes but spare ordinary taxpayers from the measures meant France's fragile economic recovery would not be jeopardised, they said.

But to keep the deficit down in the longer term, the government would have to attack the structural roots of France's budget problems and reform the pension and health care systems, as well as reduce the size of the civil service, they added.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn announced measures on Monday to cut the deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion) and keep France on course for the single currency.

The plan followed release of a government-ordered audit which showed the 1997 budget shortfall running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- well above the three percent target in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.
The measures involve 22 billion francs in extra taxes on the profits and capital gains of firms with turnover above 50 billion francs as well as 10 billion francs in spending cuts.
Corporate taxes on firms hit by the move -- about a fifth of all French companies -- were pushed up by a bigger than expected 15 percent to 41 percent.
"They've shown their determination to move toward monetary union and the decision to raise corporate taxes will not constrain the economy," said Deutsche Bank's Patrick Mange.
"But they cannot keep using these cosmetic measures to cut the deficit. They must undertake fundamental reforms."

The government's decision not to touch household revenues was good news as it "could have been very damaging for consumption," said economist Hugue de Montvallon of brokerage Oddo. But he expressed concern the government would dump its pledge to cut corporate taxes in 1999. "These things in France have a worrying tendency of becoming permanent," he said.
Shares fell sharply after the higher taxes were announced but then recovered most of their losses. Bonds were largely unaffected and the franc firmed half a centime against the mark.
"The bond market is looking at the bottom line, which is whether monetary union will be achieved and it believes it will," said one economist.

While Strauss-Kahn would not specify a deficit target for 1997, he said the measures were aimed at shaving 0.4 of a percentage point off the deficit and the gap would hit three percent of GDP in 1998. It was 4.1 percent in 1996.

Economists predicted Germany would accept a French 1997 deficit of 3.2 or 3.3 percent. Despite Germany's assertions to the contrary, its weak economic performance meant its deficit would end up at around the same level, several said.

Analysts said France had not exhausted all sources of funds and that if needed, it could tap such state agencies as the Caisse des Depots for money. "They have bought time to see what Germany does," said Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais.
"Under an optimistic scenario, they could still come in and hit 3.0 percent," he said. "They have the flexiblity down the road if they want to use the non-fiscal receipt side."

In any event, "monetary union is not going to be abandoned because one country is a couple of points above three percent," said Mange. "Everyone knows there is a margin," Christopher Potts of brokerage Chevreux de Virieu said.
Economists said the government's scope for action had been sharply curtailed by its electoral promises to boost consumption and put France's jobless back to work.
Any switch in priorities would have angered its Communist coalition allies and upset voters who remember the U-turn by the previous centre-right administration ousted seven weeks ago.
The Socialists campaigned on a pledge of no new austerity to qualify for monetary union. ($ = 6.041 French Francs)
